metadata.title: How Cursor Rules Fixed the Biggest Problems in My Daily Coding Workflow
metadata.description: Learn how defining clear Cursor rules transformed AI-generated code into clean, predictable, and production-ready engineering workflows.
metadata.subtitle: Why defining clear AI boundaries and engineering rules transformed Cursor from a code generator into a reliable engineering partner.
metadata.author: Shahid Malik
metadata.metaDescription: Learn how defining clear Cursor rules transformed AI-generated code into clean, predictable, and production-ready engineering workflows.

blocks.content: For a long time, I thought Cursor was "good enough." It helped me write code faster, fix bugs, and scaffold features quickly. But something always felt off. The code worked, yet every time I reviewed it, I felt uncomfortable merging it into a serious project.

Over time, the problems became obvious. Different modules followed different patterns. Business logic leaked into routers. Dependencies were inconsistent. Files appeared randomly, with no clear structure. The code didn't look clean, didn't feel intentional, and most importantly, didn't feel like my code.
Cursor wasn't wrong—it was simply coding based on its own assumptions, not my engineering standards.

sections.title: The Real Issue Wasn't Cursor — It Was Missing Context

blocks.content: Before using Cursor Rules, I expected Cursor to understand my project automatically. That assumption was flawed. Cursor had no idea about:

items: When it should stop and ask questions

blocks.content: Without context, Cursor optimized for task completion, not long-term code quality. The solution wasn't better prompts. It was clear rules.

sections.title: What Changed After Defining Cursor Rules

blocks.content: Once I introduced well-defined rules, the difference was immediate.
Cursor stopped:

items: Importing infrastructure code into domain logic

blocks.content: Cursor started:
For the first time, Cursor felt like a senior engineer who understood the project.
Initially, I placed all rules in a single file. That failed quickly. The rules became messy and contradictory, leading to inconsistent behavior.
The breakthrough came when I structured rules like engineering documentation:

.cursor/
  rules/
    00-core.md
    01-architecture.md
    02-backend.md
    03-database.md
    04-api.md
    05-testing.md
This hierarchy implied priority, modularized context, and made the rules intuitive—both for humans and for Cursor.
Cursor doesn't behave like a compiler. It behaves like an engineer reading documentation.
This structure alone dramatically improved predictability and trust.
Vague rules don't work. Statements like "follow clean architecture" are meaningless to an AI.
Effective rules are enforceable and explicit, for example:
Dependencies must always point inward. Infrastructure code must never be imported into domain modules. If unavoidable, stop and explain why.
Clear rules create decision boundaries, not suggestions.

sections.title: A Simple Mental Model for Rule Writing

blocks.content: Every effective rule answers at least one question:

items: What should Cursor do when unsure?

blocks.content: Rules that answer none of these are removed.
Before writing rules, I define Cursor's role. In my projects, Cursor acts as a senior backend engineer who:
This single definition drastically changed Cursor's behavior.
Without stop conditions, Cursor can unintentionally cause damage.
One critical rule:
If schema changes are required, do not implement directly. Propose a migration plan first.
This rule alone prevented multiple production risks.

sections.title: What I Never Put in Cursor Rules

blocks.content: Some things don't belong in rules:
Cursor complements tooling; it doesn't replace linters, type checkers, or migrations.
I use two checks:

items: Can another engineer make the same decisions using these rules?
Can Cursor summarize the non-negotiables correctly?

blocks.content: If not, the rules—not Cursor—are unclear.
Cursor Rules aren't about controlling AI. They're about setting clear boundaries.
When I stopped treating Cursor as a magic generator and started onboarding it like an engineer, my workflow became predictable, clean, and reliable.
I wouldn't go back.
